newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: DOWNER DEFENDS SUPPORT FOR U.S.
Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer, says the United States did what it had to do to combat what he called "abominable behaviour" by Saddam Hussein.
Mr Downer's comments follow claims by the Iraqi embassy that Australia's backing of U-S missile strikes is bad for Australia's relationship with Iraq.
Mr Downer says it's the Iraqi Government's actions that haven't been good for Australia-Iraqi relations, and Australia is not in the wrong.
He says the United States is the only superpower that can take such action to teach President Saddam Hussein a lesson.
FRENCH INVITED FOR SOUTH PACIFIC TALKS
A French Government Minister is to arrive in the Marshall Islands this weekend to resume dialogue with the South Pacific Forum.

At the end of the leaders' summit on the South Pacific island, the Forum announced that the French Minister for European Affairs, Michele Barnier, would attend talks on Sunday. The Forum spokesman, Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister, Sir Julius Chan, said the island states want to talk to France about the future clean-up of its nuclear test site and the need for a Test Ban Treaty.
The Forum also announced that Malaysia would be invited to become a dialogue partner.
Next year's Forum is to be held in the Cook Islands.
UN NUKE TREATY LOOKING HOPEFUL
Australia's ambassador to the United Nations, Richard Butler, says a treaty to ban nuclear weapons testing might be signed by the end of the month.
Australia is leading a move to have the treaty, which would end all nuclear testing once ratified, adopted.
The world's five nuclear powers - the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France - have vowed to support it.
India, one of the nations on the threshold of being a nuclear power, opposes the treaty.
Ambassador Butler says arrangements are being made to have the General Assembly meet on Monday to adopt the draft.
If that goes through, further arrangements will be made to have the treaty open for signature by September the 23rd, when many heads of government and foreign ministers will be at the UN.
CASINO INQUIRY HANGS ON LEGAL ADVICE
The Senate Committee looking into the issuing of the Victorian Casino licence is still waiting for a legal expert's opinion before deciding on the future of its inquiry.
Committee Chairman, Bruce Childs, says it could be two weeks before the committee receives the legal advice.
Senator Childs says the committee's become embroiled in complex issues about whether it can call State officials to give evidence and wants the legal opinion to clarify its powers.
It's deferred two hearings which had been scheduled for this month while it considers its future.
APEC AIMS TO BROADEN TELECOM REACH
A meeting of ministers from Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation countries has heard that cost reductions in telecommunications are possible, but are difficult in monopolies.
Communications Minister, Richard Alston, has told the Gold Coast meeting that Australia wants to participate in schemes to lower the price and increase the reach of telecommunications networks.
Senator Alston's told representatives of sixteen other countries Australia wants to encourage co-operative projects which guarantee benefits for end users.
REFUGEE STATUS APPEAL TODAY
Three Chinese women refused refugee status in Australia are claiming a Federal Court full bench ruling against them is invalid because of a technicality.
The women's lawyers will be linked from Darwin by video to the High Court in Canberra today, while they seek leave to appeal against the ruling.
They'll argue that the Federal Court didn't have the jurisdiction to hear the appeal against the refugee status decision, because the application was lodged two days late.

The women, who've been detained in Australia since arriving by boat with their families two years ago, say they had forced abortions and faced sterilisation in China, and fear further persecution if they are returned.
ACTU to redouble IR bill protests
The ACTU is to intensify its campaign against the Federal Government's Workplace Relations Bill, which is likely to be debated over the next two months in the Senate.
The decision follows the A-L-P's admission yesterday that it's failed to win Democrat support for its amendments to the bill, meaning it will be passed in some form later this year.
However, ACTU President, Jennie George, says she's not giving up yet.
Ms George has called on unions to focus their campaigns to ensure that as many amendments as possible are passed.
PERKINS TOPS IN OLYMPIC SURVEY
A survey about the viewing habits of Australians during the Atlanta Olympics shows the popularity of basketball and hockey rose in the four years since Barcelona.
Ninty-seven per cent of Australians tuned in during the Olympics, and there were no surprises about the single most popular event - the Kieran Perkins win in the 1500 metres.
Swimming was the most popular sport, followed by track and field and basketball, then gymnastics and rowing.
More than half of those surveyed rated Perkins' performance as the most memorable highlight of the games.
Next came Cathy Freeman's silver medal in the 400 metres sprint, the women's hockey final and the men's 100 metres sprint.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
